newsitem.title: FRANCE: Britain, France agree to take part in Zaire relief.
newsitem.headline: Britain, France agree to take part in Zaire relief.

text.p: Britain and France agreed on Friday to take part in international relief efforts for refugees trapped by fighting in Zaire, and Prime Minister John Major said Britain might agree to send troops.

The deal, reached at a bilateral summit, partly patched up discord over a Franco-Spanish plan for an international force of 5,000 troops to help 1.2 million Hutu refugees trapped by fighting in eastern Zaire.

"The two countries have agreed to coordinate their efforts closely...so that the necessary international arrangements can swiftly be put into place to enable humanitarian aid reliably to reach displaced persons and refugees in Zaire once again," a joint statement said.
"They are ready to contribute to this," it added. That phrase was initially omitted from the English version of the statement in what British officials dismissed as a typing error.

The statement did not spell out whether the action would involve troops. Earlier, Major had said "it is certainly possible" that British troops could be sent to Zaire though he added it was still not clear this was the right thing to do.
France accused the world this week of being "spineless" in its reaction to the crisis in Zaire. Britain has so far been non-committal.
"We have had a good reaction from the Spanish and the Italians during the last few days," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said in Bordeaux.
"The British are more hesitant over whether to send troops but I nevertheless feel that they are also determined to work with us to solve this problem," he added.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman in Paris said France wanted the force to be one-third African, one-third American and one-third European.

France and Spain have said they could send 1,000 troops each as part of a 5,000-strong force. They want U.N. approval for the plan, designed to help Hutu refugees left without food by the fighting between Zairean troops and Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels.

"I have no doubt that Britain may be involved in some way, whether it is logistic support, whether it is financial support, whether possibly even it is troop support," Major told BBC radio. "I don't rule that out."

He said, however, that a series of international consultations were needed first. Major's joint statement with Chirac said that the longer-term objective was "enabling the voluntary return of (refugees) to their country of origin".
They said preparations for a regional peace conference should begin as soon as possible under the aegis of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).

In a string of interviews to the British media, Major also stressed there would be no change in the British government's policy towards the single European currency. Chirac would like Britain to join in a first wave from 1999 but London is keeping its options open.
"No one can rule that out," Major said of the possibility of joining from 1999. "We can decide to take it or we can decide not to take it but there is a huge amount to be settled."
In his interviews, the prime minister also hinted that London might snarl up progress on the intergovernmental conference reviewing EU institutions ahead of enlargement of the 15-nation bloc.

With a ruling from the European Court expected next week on the 48-hour maximum working week directive, he said the Advocate General's opinion, delivered months ago, suggested Britain might lose the case and risk having the restrictions imposed upon it.
"I think we have to say, if we lose this case, it is not acceptable," he said.
